verdict.rationale: ScrapingBee's own API lets developers control when HTML is returned. The `wait_for` CSS/XPath selector holds the response until an element appears, and JS scenarios can insert explicit waits before the HTML comes back. Developers can also trade completeness for speed by blocking resources or ads. However, the pack does not document the full latency-versus-completeness control surface, so the evidence falls short of complete story coverage. Missing for 10: a documented fixed-delay wait parameter outside JS scenarios, network-idle/browser-load wait conditions, request timeout controls, and independent or hands-on corroboration of the latency tradeoff.

support.subject: As a developer, I can trade off latency against completeness by controlling exactly when content is returned

citations.quote: Our headless browsers will wait for the CSS / Xpath selector passed in the parameter before returning the HTML.
If you want to interact with pages you want to scrape before we return your the HTML you can add JavaScript scenario to your API call.
By default, and to speed up requests, ScrapingBee blocks all images and CSS in the scraped page, but to scrape them, use `block_resources=false`
To avoid scraping them (e.g.,to speed up your request), use `block_ads=true`
